titleText.es: Hay que preparar a los niños para esta peculiar explicación; es muy común y está completamente equivocada. Buenas frases son
titleText.en: This is a fun explanation to prepare your kids for; it's common and totally wrong. Good lines include 'why does the air have to travel on both sides at the same time?' and 'I saw the Wright brothers plane and those wings were curved the same on the top and bottom!'
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish source manifest ends after “Buenas frases son ” because the archive page places unescaped quotation marks inside its HTML title attribute. The raw HTML continues with intended Spanish versions of the two quoted examples in the complete official title text. The manifest-truncated Spanish value and the complete official English title text are preserved exactly. OCR also interleaved every panel, split true line-wrapped words, split SUSTENTACIÓN into SUS and TENTACIÓN, read VA as YA, and omitted the accents in PRESIÓN and REVÉS. The visibly duplicated DE DE is a source typo and is transcribed as two lexical occurrences.

regions.labelEs: CÓMO MANEJAR A UN ESTUDIANTE QUE DESAFÍA TU EXPERIENCIA CON UNA PREGUNTA PERSPICAZ.

applications.explanationEn: CÓMO introduces the type of action being explained, and MANEJAR stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
A marks the person directly affected by MANEJAR, and UN ESTUDIANTE completes that person phrase.
ESTUDIANTE names the person, QUE opens the added description, and DESAFÍA TU EXPERIENCIA supplies the information about that person.
PERSPICAZ describes the feminine singular noun PREGUNTA; this adjective keeps the same singular form for either gender.
The neutral descriptive adjective PERSPICAZ follows the noun PREGUNTA.

regions.labelEs: BIEN, CHICOS, EL AIRE DE DE ARRIBA VIAJA UNA DISTANCIA MAYOR, POR LO QUE TIENE QUE IR MÁS RÁPIDO. EL AIRE QUE VA MÁS RÁPIDO EJERCE UNA PRESIÓN MENOR, POR LO QUE EL ALA RECIBE SUSTENTACIÓN HACIA ARRIBA.

applications.explanationEn: MAYOR describes the feminine singular noun DISTANCIA and uses its gender-invariant singular form.
The descriptive comparison MAYOR follows DISTANCIA in neutral noun-plus-description order.
POR LO QUE introduces the consequence of the preceding comparison.
TIENE changes for the singular subject, QUE links the construction, and IR remains in dictionary form.
RÁPIDO describes how the movement IR happens; MÁS increases its degree.
MÁS raises the degree of the manner word RÁPIDO.
AIRE names the thing being described, QUE opens the added information, and VA MÁS RÁPIDO states what that air does.
RÁPIDO describes how VA happens and stays in its unchanged masculine singular form.
MÁS raises the degree of RÁPIDO without stating the other side of the comparison.
MENOR describes the feminine singular noun PRESIÓN and keeps its gender-invariant singular form.
The descriptive comparison MENOR follows the noun PRESIÓN.
This second POR LO QUE likewise introduces a claimed consequence.
ALA remains feminine, but its opening stressed a sound makes singular EL the article immediately before it.

regions.labelEs: ¿ENTONCES CÓMO PUEDEN VIAJAR DEL REVÉS LOS AVIONES?

applications.explanationEn: CÓMO carries a written accent because it directly asks for the way something can happen.
PUEDEN changes for the plural subject, while VIAJAR stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
DEL REVÉS marks the planes' orientation as upside down.

regions.labelEs: VAYA, ¡BUENA PREGUNTA! QUIZÁS ESTA IMAGEN ESTÁ SIMPLIFICADA, ¡O EQUIVOCADA! DEBEMOS APRENDER MÁS.

applications.explanationEn: BUENA uses its feminine singular ending to match PREGUNTA.
The overall positive evaluation BUENA appears before the noun PREGUNTA.
QUIZÁS presents the possibility, while ESTÁ keeps the ordinary statement form.
Both SIMPLIFICADA and EQUIVOCADA use feminine singular -a endings to describe IMAGEN.
ESTÁ introduces two coordinated completed-action forms that describe the image's possible state.
DEBEMOS changes for “we,” while APRENDER remains in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: ES... COMPLICADO. Y TENEMOS QUE CONTINUAR.

applications.explanationEn: TENEMOS changes for “we,” QUE links the construction, and CONTINUAR stays in dictionary form.
SON uses SER to identify who the Reyes really are in this claim.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what, how, or where to do something without naming a new person who does it?
cards.answerEn: Use an accented question word, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This compact pattern is used when the person who would perform the action is already clear from context. The question word keeps its written accent even inside a larger statement: qué hacer, cómo llegar, dónde aparcar.

example.en: I do not know where to park.

cards.noteEn: Besides meaning “to drive” in much of Latin America, manejar can mean managing or dealing with a person, problem, or situation.

example.en: She knows how to handle difficult situations.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a person-denoting object
cards.noteEn: The personal a also appears before words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) when they directly receive an action, even though they do not identify one specific individual.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.
Estudiante can refer to a male or female student; the surrounding article or other context can show gender when it matters.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Desafía is a present-time form of desafiar for one person or thing.

example.es: La nueva prueba desafía esa teoría.
example.en: The new evidence challenges that theory.

cards.noteEn: Pregunta is a feminine noun when it names a question. The same spelling can also be a command meaning ‘ask’; context distinguishes the two uses.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.
Perspicaz has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

cards.answerEn: guys; everyone (informal address to a group)
cards.noteEn: Chicos literally refers to boys or young men, but speakers can use it informally to get the attention of a male or mixed group, much like ‘guys’ in English.

cards.promptEs: distancia mayor · aire más rápido · presión menor · del revés
cards.questionEn: Why does the upside-down-flight question expose a problem with this explanation of lift?
cards.answerEn: The explanation assumes that air split by a wing must reunite at the trailing edge at the same time, but air has no such equal-transit-time requirement.
cards.noteEn: Different airflow speeds and pressures do matter for lift, but the common story that air over the longer curved surface must hurry to meet the air below is false. Lift depends on the complete flow around the wing, including its shape, circulation, and angle of attack. Aircraft can produce lift while inverted by using an appropriate angle of attack, so upside-down flight is a useful counterexample to the oversimplified story.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; this de is an accidental duplicate
cards.noteEn: An accidental written repetition of de does not add meaning: one copy is redundant. This kind of editing error should be removed in normal Spanish.

example.es: El borrador decía «de de Madrid»; debe decir «de Madrid».
example.en: The draft said ‘de de Madrid’; it should say ‘de Madrid.’

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links a noun to arriba, ‘above’ or ‘upper’
cards.noteEn: De arriba can identify the person or thing located above another reference point. Natural English may use “above,” “upstairs,” or put “upper” before the noun.

example.es: La ventana de arriba está abierta.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por lo que

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a fact to its consequence with “so” or “which is why”?
cards.answerEn: Use por lo que before the consequence.
cards.noteEn: Por lo que looks back at the fact just mentioned and introduces what follows from it. The three words work together as one result connector.

example.es: Perdí el autobús, por lo que llegué tarde.
example.en: I missed the bus, which is why I arrived late.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por lo que
no separate English word; part of a result connector

cards.promptEs: tener que + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener, then que, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only tener changes for the person and time: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, and so on. The final action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes tener que, “to have to”
to go; to work or run
cards.noteEn: Ir normally means “to go.” In ir bien or ir mal, it describes how something works or is going: va bien means “it works” or “it’s going well.”

cards.promptEs: verbo + adjetivo usado para describir el modo
cards.questionEn: How can words such as claro, alto, or profundo describe how an action is done without adding -mente?
cards.answerEn: In certain common combinations, put the describing word after the verb and keep it in its masculine singular form.
cards.noteEn: A word that normally describes a noun can sometimes work like an English -ly word and describe the action instead: hablar claro, volar alto, respirar profundo. It does not change for the person doing the action. This use is conventional, so it cannot be applied freely to every adjective.

cards.promptEs: más + palabra que describe cómo se hace algo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action is done faster, more slowly, or more carefully?
cards.answerEn: Put más before the word that describes how the action is done.
cards.noteEn: Más raises the degree of a manner word. Spanish can use an unchanged form such as rápido or despacio, or an adverb ending in -mente. The other side of the comparison does not have to be stated.
Va is the present-time form of ir for one person or thing.
Menor compares an amount, size, or degree. It has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.es: Esta opción tiene un coste menor.
example.en: This option has a lower cost.

cards.promptEs: el agua · el habla · del águila (nombres femeninos)
cards.questionEn: Which singular article is used immediately before a feminine noun that begins with a stressed a sound?
cards.answerEn: Use el immediately before that singular noun; use del when de + el contracts.
cards.noteEn: The noun remains feminine. Describing words still use feminine forms, and the plural uses las: el agua fría, las aguas frías. The rule applies only when the stressed a sound begins the noun.

example.es: El águila blanca voló sobre el agua fría.
example.en: The white eagle flew over the cold water.

cards.noteEn: Ala is feminine, but singular el is used immediately before it because the word begins with a stressed a sound: el ala. The plural is las alas.
In aviation, sustentación is the upward aerodynamic force that helps support an aircraft.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.answerEn: they can; they are able to

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins del revés, ‘upside down’ or ‘inside out’
cards.noteEn: Del is the contraction of de + el, but in del revés the two words function together as a fixed orientation expression.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is upside down, inside out, or the wrong way around?
cards.answerEn: Use del revés after the thing or action whose orientation is reversed.
cards.noteEn: Del revés is a fixed expression. Its natural English wording depends on the object: a picture may be “upside down,” clothing may be “inside out,” and an ordered sequence may be “backward.”

cards.answerEn: upside down; inside out (as part of del revés)
cards.noteEn: In del revés, revés marks an inverted or reversed orientation.

example.en: You are wearing your T-shirt inside out.

cards.noteEn: As a judgment on an answer, choice, or response, bien can label it as correct. This differs from bien meaning “well” or opening a reply as “all right.”
Buena is the feminine singular form of bueno. It is used before or after a feminine singular noun, such as práctica or decisión.

cards.questionEn: Where do common judgment words such as bueno or malo often go?
cards.answerEn: Put them before the noun when they give an overall evaluation: buena idea, mala noticia.
cards.noteEn: Spanish often puts a neutral descriptive word after its noun, but common evaluation words can come before it. The describing word still changes to match the noun: bueno becomes buena before a feminine singular noun.

cards.questionEn: How can you say “maybe” while presenting an idea as a neutral or fairly plausible possibility?
cards.answerEn: Put quizás before the idea and use the verb form you would use in an ordinary statement.
cards.noteEn: This ordinary statement form is called the indicative: es stays es, and tiene stays tiene. Spanish can instead use a special possibility form called the subjunctive after quizás when the speaker wants to emphasize uncertainty; quizás alone does not force either choice.

cards.promptEs: estar + forma de acción completada que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe the state something is in as the result of an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by the action's completed form, with an ending that matches the thing being described.
cards.noteEn: The completed form, often ending in -ado or -ido, is also called a participle. Estar changes for who or what is in the state. The participle changes like a describing word: cerrado, cerrada, cerrados, or cerradas. This pattern focuses on the resulting state, not on who performed the action.
Simplificada is the completed-action form of simplificar used as a description. Its -a ending matches a feminine singular noun.
Equivocada describes a feminine singular person or thing as mistaken or incorrect.
Debemos is the present “we” form of deber. Before an unchanged action verb, it expresses advice or obligation.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should or must do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only deber changes for the person and time. Depending on context, deber can sound like advice, duty, or a strong requirement.
After estar, mal can describe something as wrong, incorrect, or not as it should be. English uses the adjective ‘wrong,’ even though mal often works like an adverb in Spanish.
Spanish can begin an impersonal evaluation with es plus a describing word. English normally supplies an impersonal ‘it,’ but Spanish does not add a separate subject word.

example.en: It is strange that it is raining.

cards.noteEn: Capitalized Los Reyes commonly refers to the Three Kings, or Magi. In Spain and other Spanish-speaking traditions, children may receive gifts from them around 6 January; their gift-bringing role is culturally comparable to Santa Claus.

example.es: Los Reyes traen regalos en enero.
example.en: The Three Kings bring gifts in January.

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.
